Chapter 3: The Two-Part Decoupled Storage Law (pagerecord.bejson vs pages_db/<uuid>.json)

Here is where amateur CMS developers humiliate themselves: they stuff 50,000 words of HTML content, markdown bodies, and raw code snippets directly into the main table rows. Then they wonder why running SELECT * FROM posts causes their process to spike to 4GB of RAM and grind their server to a halt.

In BEJSON CMS, we enforce the Two-Part Decoupled Storage Law:

TWO-PART STORAGE INVARIANT: Global catalog matrices hold routing metadata ONLY. Content payloads live in isolated single-record polymorphic stores indexed by UUID.

Look at the separation of concerns:

  1. Part 1: The Master Catalog (storage/mfdb/site_master/data/pagerecord.bejson): Contains strictly indexed metadata: page_uuid, page_title, page_slug, page_cat_name, page_type, page_created_at, and page_featured_img. The entire table for the whole blog weighs under 6KB! The static publisher can ingest, filter, sort, and paginate all articles in less than 3 milliseconds without ever touching a single paragraph of article body text.
  2. Part 2: The Content Vault (storage/mfdb/pages_db/<uuid>.json): Each article owns its own isolated 104db container. When the publisher compiles an article page, it performs a targeted POSIX open on that specific UUID file only: 
    {
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104db",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Records_Type": ["PageMeta", "Content"],
  "Fields": [
    {"name": "Record_Type_Parent", "type": "string"},

Result? You can store 100,000 articles in pages_db/ without degrading the memory footprint or search speed of the primary catalog by even 1 microsecond. That is real architectural separation of concerns, not corporate marketing cope.

Chapter 4: The Invariant $O(1)$ Field-Map Cache — Eliminating Positional Blindness

Every novice developer who looks at BEJSON asks the same skid question: "Wait, if values are positional arrays, what happens if I change the column order? Won't my code break?"

Only if you write garbage code. In the Elton Boehnen ecosystem, Policy §3.2 explicitly outlaws positional hardcoding under strict negative constraints. You NEVER write row[1] or row[3].

Instead, all BEJSON access is mediated by the Mandatory $O(1)$ Field-Map Cache. Look at how src/lib/lib_bejson_CMS_md2html.py resolves fields:

# Load table and compile O(1) name-to-index lookup cache
bejson_doc = json.loads(pagerecord_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
fields_list = bejson_doc.get("Fields", [])

# Build O(1) memory hash map
field_map = {f["name"]: idx for idx, f in enumerate(fields_list)}

# Now access row values purely by canonical column name in O(1) time:
for row in bejson_doc.get("Values", []):
    uuid       = row[field_map["page_uuid"]]
    title      = row[field_map["page_title"]]
    slug       = row[field_map["page_slug"]]
    created_at = row[field_map["page_created_at"]]
    feat_img   = row[field_map["page_featured_img"]]

Do you understand why this is superior to standard dictionary JSON? Let's break down the computational complexity and memory footprint:

Storage Paradigm Memory Allocation per Row Key Duplication Bloat Schema Evolution Resistance
Standard Dict Array (JSON) Heavy Python dict overhead (~232 bytes per row) 100% key string repetition on EVERY row Medium (Keys can desync between rows)
BEJSON + O(1) Field Map Lightweight tuple/list (~56 bytes per row) 0% key repetition (Declared ONCE in header) Absolute (Field map dynamically binds column order)

You can reorder columns in Fields, insert 10 new columns at any index, and existing reader scripts will resolve the exact same values without modifying a single line of logic. That is mathematical invariance.

Chapter 5: The Build Engine (BEJSON_CMS_Publisher.py) — Deterministic Edge Compilation

How does raw tabular BEJSON turn into high-speed static HTML? Look at src/web/BEJSON_CMS_Publisher.py. It doesn't invoke Webpack. It doesn't invoke Babel. It doesn't download 4,000 npm dependencies. It is a single, zero-dependency Python script running strictly on stdlib.

Here is the exact build execution pipeline executed whenever you run cms-manage.py publish:

  1. Stage 1: Manifest & Config Resolution: The publisher instantiates site_master/104a.mfdb.bejson, resolves siteconfig.bejson (extracting site title, base URL, creator credits), and indexes Category, NavLink, and SocialLink.
  2. Stage 2: Deterministic Asset Synchronization: Every file in storage/mfdb/assets/ is mirrored into storage/builds/assets/. Vector SVGs, high-DPI PNGs, and compressed WebP hero graphics are verified against SHA-256 fingerprints in mediaasset.bejson to prevent stale asset caches.
  3. Stage 3: Page Synthesis & Skeleton Hydration: For every row in pagerecord.bejson, the publisher loads the isolated pages_db/<uuid>.json body, applies the chosen Jinja/HTML template (post.html or Global_Skeleton.html), injects active sidebar categories, navigation items, social links, and wraps the content in clean semantic HTML5 markup.
  4. Stage 4: Feeds & SEO Topology: Compiles storage/builds/index.html (the responsive 7-card home feed), category feeds (/blog/bejson/index.html, /blog/projects/index.html), the standalone apps index, robots.txt, and a canonical sitemap.xml with ISO 8601 timestamps.

Every graphic adheres strictly to the Tri-Color Design Standard:

2. The Zero-Jump Mobile Touch Calibration

Most embedded canvas tools break completely on mobile devices: when a user tries to scroll down the page, touch gestures get swallowed by canvas pan event listeners, causing viewport stutter and accidental coordinate jumps.

We solved this cleanly at the DOM coordinate layer with passive touch interception:

// Surgical Touch Isolation Protocol
canvasContainer.addEventListener('touchstart', (event) => {
  if (event.touches.length === 1) {
    // Single touch allows natural document scrolling
    allowDocumentScroll(true);
  } else if (event.touches.length === 2) {
    // Two-finger pinch triggers spatial zoom/pan
    event.preventDefault();
    handleSpatialPinchPan(event);
